name: South Sudan
card_headline: South Sudan has moved its first election to February 2027 with Machar under house arrest, the unity government dissolved and four counties at risk of famine
card_summary: South Sudan's first election since independence, due on 22 December 2026, has been moved to 11 February 2027, and the electoral commission gave no reason. President Salva Kiir dissolved the unity government in September. First Vice President Riek Machar has been under house arrest since March 2025 and is on trial. Fighting between the army and Machar's forces has displaced hundreds of thousands in Jonglei and Upper Nile. The IPC counts 7.8 million people in acute food insecurity and sees famine risk in four counties.
card_local: Eye Radio, Radio Tamazuj and Sudans Post cover the election timetable, the Machar trial and the opposition's refusal to allow registration in areas it holds.[1][2][3]
card_international: AFP and AP report the move to 11 February 2027 and that registration began the same day with equipment still arriving.[4][5][6]
card_scholar: ISS argued in September that credible elections were no longer possible, and ACLED found the 2018 peace agreement not viable in its current form.[7][8]
context_md: South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, and a civil war from 2013 to 2018 killed at least 400,000 people.[4] The 2018 peace agreement created a power-sharing government under President Salva Kiir.[9] Riek Machar was first vice president until he was suspended in 2025.[10] Elections were first expected in 2022 and have been postponed several times since.[9] Machar was placed under house arrest in March 2025, and his supporters and government forces have been in escalating clashes since.[4][7] On 22 September 2026 Kiir dissolved the unity government and named a caretaker administration.[9] The electoral commission then moved the vote from 22 December 2026 to 11 February 2027.[4]

sections.title: The election slipped to February 2027 after the government dissolved itself
sections.body_md:
South Sudan's electoral commission announced on 14 November that the first national vote since independence would move from 22 December 2026 to 11 February 2027. It gave no reason.[4] The campaign is set to run from 27 December to 9 February, with results announced four days after the vote.[4][6] Voter registration opened the same day and runs to 28 November, with 3,161 centres and more than 22,000 staff.[4] AFP reported that officials said not all the necessary equipment had reached the centres.[6] About 90 percent of the country's 15 million people lack state-recognised identification, according to the World Bank as cited by AFP.[4]

The delay follows a series of moves by President Salva Kiir. On 22 September he dissolved the transitional unity government, dismissed all vice presidents, ministers and local administrators, and dissolved the national and state assemblies. The judiciary and security institutions stayed in place.[9] The decree says Kiir remains in office until an elected president takes over.[9] The day before, parliament had amended the National Elections Act so that a permanent constitution and a census no longer have to come first.[9] The ISS dates amendments removing those preconditions to 22 July 2026.[7] Kiir also replaced the elections commission's head the week before the dissolution.[9]

Reactions split. Amnesty International called the decree a "decisive step" toward the first elections.[9] Yasmin Sooka, who chairs the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, called the changes a "constitutional coup through legislative reforms" in October.[4] Outlets count earlier postponements differently: Al Jazeera says at least three, while ISS and The East African say five.[4][7][11] Radio Tamazuj reports that the transitional period under the 2018 agreement is due to end in February 2027.[3]

lenses.local: Radio Tamazuj quoted the University of Juba's Abraham Kuol Nyuon in August saying that without voters there is no election, and that parties looked unprepared.[3]
lenses.international: AFP and AP carried the 14 November postponement, and AFP quoted rights campaigner Malong Deng saying there are no real elections in South Sudan.[4][5][6]
lenses.scholar: ISS researchers wrote in September that polls under current conditions would produce an illegitimate government, and that Kiir may be preparing another extension.[7]

sections.title: The war the 2018 deal was meant to end has returned to Jonglei, Upper Nile and Unity
sections.body_md:
Fighting between the army (SSPDF) and forces loyal to Riek Machar's SPLM/A-IO has spread since Machar's arrest. ACLED reported that between 1 December 2025 and 23 January 2026 violence killed at least 200 people in Jonglei state, among them no fewer than 40 civilians, and that more than 230,000 people left their homes. It lists clashes in Jonglei, Upper Nile, Unity and parts of Equatoria.[8]

On 6 March the SSPDF issued a 72-hour directive to vacate Akobo County. OCHA says Akobo was then fully inaccessible to humanitarians, its hospital was looted, and MSF evacuated its team on 7 March.[12] OCHA recorded 134 access incidents in January and February and four aid workers killed in Jonglei.[12] The IOM-verified displacement figure it cites is more than 267,000 people across four states, and about 100,000 people crossed into Ethiopia.[12]

The ceasefire monitoring body CTSAMVM logged 76 alleged violations in a report covered on 21 January, including airstrikes in Ulang, Nasir and Jonglei in November and December 2025, and a strike on Lankien on 29 December with reported civilian deaths.[13] Amnesty says armed men from Mayom County stormed Abiemnom town in Unity State on 1 March 2026 and killed and injured hundreds within a few hours. That is Amnesty's account and this draft found no second source.[14] The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan warned in February of a risk of "a return to full-scale war" and described a shift to air strikes on civilian-populated areas.[15]

lenses.local: Sudans Post reported the ceasefire monitors' tally, and Radio Tamazuj reported that the embassies of nine countries including Japan called for an immediate halt to fighting in January.[13][10]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports the UN Commission's February warning, including that government forces and Ugandan troops carried out aerial bombardments.[15]
lenses.scholar: ACLED concludes that the 2018 peace agreement is no longer viable in its current form.[8]

sections.title: Machar has been held for twenty months, and the opposition has split over the vote
sections.body_md:
Riek Machar has been under house arrest since March 2025.[4] Machar and eight other SPLM/A-IO members were charged on 11 September 2025 with murder, treason, crimes against humanity and other offences tied to the White Army's attack on the Nasir garrison.[10] Machar denies the charges.[9]

The trial runs before a Special Court in Juba. Eye Radio reported the 46th session on 2 February 2026, with Judge James Alala presiding. The prosecution's final witness, a South African cyber expert, testified about phones examined in the case. Defence lawyers complained of "humiliating treatment" of the seven detained co-accused during searches, and the prosecutor said there was no evidence for the claim.[1] AFP's November report gave no trial date or details of proceedings.[6]

The opposition is divided. On 22 June the SPLM-IO's acting chairman, Nathaniel Pierino, said voter registration officials and campaigners would not be allowed in SPLA-IO-held areas and would be treated as prisoners of war or worse. Only Sudans Post carried this statement, and the Elections Commission had not responded.[2] On 30 June a breakaway faction led by Peacebuilding Minister Stephen Par Kuol was recorded as the IO Party.[16] Smaller parties objected to a $75,000 registration fee, and the Political Parties Council chair, James Akol Zakayo, called the 30 June deadline final.[17]

lenses.local: Radio Tamazuj and Sudans Post report on the registration fee, the breakaway IO Party and Pierino's warning.[17][16][2]
lenses.international: AFP and Al Jazeera describe Machar's detention and the charges against him but give no trial details beyond the existing allegations.[6][9]
lenses.scholar: ISS calls for international pressure for Machar's release and a time-bound, consensual extension with a roadmap to elections.[7]

sections.title: Uganda's troops and the Sudan war have made South Sudan's neighbours part of the fight
sections.body_md:
Ugandan forces entered South Sudan in March 2025 to support Kiir's government. A UN Commission report found that joint South Sudanese and Ugandan aerial bombardments targeted civilian-populated areas, mainly affecting Nuer communities in opposition-affiliated areas, with improvised incendiary devices.[18] Uganda denied taking part in combat operations. It says its troops are there at the government's invitation under a bilateral security agreement.[18] Amnesty says the Ugandan deployment broke the UN arms embargo. The Security Council renewed the embargo for another year in May, and some members abstained.[14]

The Sudan war reaches South Sudan through its oil and its borders. The RSF captured the Heglig oilfield on 8 December 2025 and Sudanese army units retreated into South Sudan. South Sudan's army chief of staff, Paul Nang, said troops entered Heglig on 10 December under a tripartite deal involving Kiir, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Hemedti. About 3,900 Sudanese soldiers crossed into Rubkona County, according to Unity State officials.[19] Heglig has a central processing facility that can handle up to 130,000 barrels a day of South Sudanese crude.[19]

South Sudan also hosts people fleeing Sudan. The joint NGO letter cites 598,467 registered refugees as of 30 November 2025, of whom 567,801 were from Sudan.[20] OCHA counts nearly 1.3 million refugees and returnees arriving from Sudan since April 2023, with about 380,000 more projected in 2026.[21]

lenses.international: AP reports the UN Commission's findings and Uganda's denial. Al Jazeera reports the Heglig deployment as described by South Sudan's army.[18][19]
lenses.scholar: Coventry University's Jan Pospisil told Al Jazeera that Sudan's army wants to deny the RSF a revenue stream at Heglig.[19]

sections.title: Oil pays for almost everything, and it leaves through a country at war
sections.body_md:
Eye Radio's June analysis says oil provides roughly 90 to 95 percent of government income, and that exports travel through Sudan to Port Sudan. The pipeline disruption that began in February 2024 reportedly cost about $7 million a day, and oil resumed flowing on 7 January 2025.[22] The same article reports that the pound lost nearly 200 percent of its value within one fiscal year and that the FY2025/26 budget is 4.172 trillion pounds. It cites the World Bank for a poverty rate of 92 percent in March 2025.[22]

The World Bank's February 2026 Public Finance Review says public spending averages 35 percent of GDP and is skewed toward administration, security and the rule of law. It reports widespread salary arrears and "extreme oil dependence". It recommends paying all oil revenue into the National Revenue Fund, publishing quarterly oil data and paying salaries monthly.[23] An older Eye Radio report from December 2024 said civil servants and the armed forces had gone 11 months without pay.[24]

The UN Commission said in September that there had been no progress on corruption since its report a year earlier, and accused government elites of stealing billions of dollars in oil revenue. That is the Commission's finding, and the government rejected its wider assessment of election conditions.[25][7] Climate adds cost: the World Bank says flooding covers up to a quarter of the country in severe years and that adaptation will need more than $13 billion by 2050.[23]

lenses.local: Eye Radio ties the economic collapse to the 2024 pipeline shutdown and the pound's fall.[22]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports that Heglig threatens both Sudan's and South Sudan's main revenue source if fighting continues.[19]
lenses.scholar: The World Bank's Public Finance Review names extreme oil dependence and governance gaps as the source of volatility.[23]

sections.title: 7.8 million people are acutely hungry and four counties are at risk of famine
sections.body_md:
The IPC's April 2026 projection update puts 7.8 million people, 55 percent of the 14.2 million analysed, in IPC Phase 3 or worse for April to July. That is about 280,000 more than in September 2025.[26] Some 2.5 million are in Phase 4 (emergency), and about 73,000 are in Phase 5 (catastrophe) in Akobo, Fangak, Nyirol and Uror in Jonglei and Nasir and Ulang in Upper Nile.[26] Four counties are at risk of famine, up from one in the previous analysis: Nasir and Ulang in Upper Nile, and Nyirol and Akobo in Jonglei.[26]

The IPC counts 2.2 million children aged 6 to 59 months needing treatment for acute malnutrition, including about 697,000 with severe acute malnutrition.[26] OCHA reports 100,646 cholera cases and 1,652 deaths since 28 September 2024.[12] The 2026 response plan says more than 10 million people, about two thirds of the population, are projected to need assistance.[21]

Displacement counts differ by source. The UN Commission says displacement rose nearly 40 percent last year to 3.2 million people, with about 280,000 displaced since late December.[15] UNHCR's year-end 2025 report lists 2.4 million South Sudanese refugees in neighbouring countries, 1.3 million internally displaced people and 199,000 returned refugees. It received $130 million of the $493 million it needed.[27]

lenses.local: Eye Radio repeats the IPC figures and adds an October 2025 cholera count of more than 95,000 cases.[22]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera cites the UN Commission on displacement of 3.2 million people and nearly 10 million needing aid.[15]
lenses.scholar: The IPC is the main technical source on famine risk, and its four-county risk is up from one county in the earlier analysis.[26]

sections.title: A cybercrime law, entrenched impunity and a UN finding the government rejects
sections.body_md:
President Kiir signed the Cybercrimes and Computer Misuse Act, 2026 on 18 February. CPJ says it punishes "false or misleading" information and damage to reputation with up to five years in prison, and lets the National Communication Authority order internet providers to hand over data without judicial oversight.[28] Officials say the law addresses online fraud and digital harassment, and the Information Minister, Ateny Wek, did not respond to CPJ.[28] CPJ has documented at least 10 journalists killed in South Sudan since 2012, and says authorities suspended social media access and the online outlet Hot in Juba in 2025.[28] Radio Tamazuj relayed the CPJ call for a review.[29]

The UN Commission reported in February that civic space has deteriorated sharply, with journalists, activists and opposition figures facing harassment and arbitrary detention.[15] A joint letter from 129 organisations cites arbitrary arrest, surveillance and intimidation by the National Security Service.[20]

On 10 September the Commission said the country lacked many of the safeguards for peaceful and credible polls, and ISS reports that the government rejected that assessment.[7] Commissioner Carlos Castresana Fernandez said impunity "becomes entrenched, and that breeds violence."[30] The Commission found conflict-related sexual violence continuing, and Amnesty says it goes unpunished.[15][14]

lenses.local: Radio Tamazuj reports CPJ's call for the cybercrime law to be reviewed and James Bidal's warning of self-censorship.[29]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Africanews report the Commission's findings on civic space and corruption.[15][25]
lenses.scholar: Jurist summarises the Commission's finding that justice institutions are weak and underfunded and that perpetrators are rarely held accountable.[30]

timeline.text: South Sudan becomes independent from Sudan.
Civil war begins and runs to 2018, killing at least 400,000 people.
A peace agreement creates the power-sharing government.
Riek Machar is placed under house arrest, and Ugandan forces enter South Sudan.
Machar and eight other SPLM/A-IO members are charged with murder, treason and other offences.
The RSF captures Heglig; South Sudanese troops deploy there on 10 December.
Opposition forces announce the fall of Pajut in Jonglei.
Kiir signs the Cybercrimes and Computer Misuse Act, 2026.
The UN Commission on Human Rights warns of a return to full-scale war.
The army orders civilians and aid groups to leave Akobo County within 72 hours.
IPC publishes its update: 7.8 million acutely food insecure, four counties at famine risk.
The SPLM-IO's acting chairman says registration officials will not be allowed in its areas.
A breakaway SPLM-IO faction is registered as the IO Party.
The UN Commission says the country lacks safeguards for credible polls.
Kiir dissolves the unity government and the legislatures and names a caretaker administration.
The electoral commission moves the election to 11 February 2027 and opens voter registration.

scores.coverage_basis: AFP, AP and Reuters file on South Sudan around big political events such as the election delay and the government's dissolution, with little steady wire flow between them[4][5][9]. Specialist research from ACLED, ISS and the IPC is regular, and Juba outlets such as Eye Radio, Radio Tamazuj and Sudans Post publish daily[8][7][1].

severity.basis: ACLED reports at least 200 killed in Jonglei in under two months, and the UN Commission warns of a return to full-scale war with air strikes on civilian areas[8][15].
The IPC counts 7.8 million people in Phase 3 or worse, about 73,000 in Phase 5 and four counties at risk of famine, and OCHA counts a cholera toll of 1,652 deaths[26][12].
The legislature and cabinet were dissolved in September, the first vice president is on trial and a cybercrime law carries up to five years for false information[9][1][28].
Oil is 90 to 95 percent of government income, the pound reportedly lost nearly 200 percent in a year, and the World Bank reports widespread salary arrears[22][23].
Famine-risk counties rose from one to four, the unity government was dissolved and the vote was moved again[26][9][4].

parts.basis: Uganda has deployed troops and Western embassies and Japan press for a ceasefire, but this draft found no source on US, Chinese or Russian forces or deals[18][10].
South Sudanese crude exits through Sudan's pipelines, and Heglig alone can process up to 130,000 barrels a day[19].
About 100,000 people crossed into Ethiopia, 2.4 million South Sudanese are refugees abroad, and Sudan's war has reached the oilfields on the border[12][27][19].
Refugees abroad number 2.4 million, and South Sudan hosts more than 598,000 refugees, most from Sudan[27][20].
A UN arms embargo is in force and the UN Commission says Uganda's role raises concern about violations, while the 2018 settlement is being dismantled[14][15][9].

summary: South Sudan matters beyond its borders through refugee flows, the oil that moves through Sudan's war zone and Uganda's military role, rather than through trade or great-power rivalry[27][19][18].
gi.up: A collapse of the pipeline route through Sudan, a large new outflow of refugees, or confirmed great-power basing or arms deals.
gi.down: A credible election with Machar's release and a revived power-sharing arrangement.

gaps: No published reason for the election postponement was found; the electoral commission's own statement was not located and AFP, AP and Al Jazeera all report that none was given.
Local sourcing is solid on politics and the trial but thin on the economy and on states outside Juba; Eye Radio, Radio Tamazuj and Sudans Post were read through single articles, not systematically.
No source on the role of the United States, China, Russia or Gulf states in South Sudan was read, so the great-power score rests on Uganda and the Troika embassies.
The 1 March 2026 Abiemnom attack rests on Amnesty alone; the 22 July 2026 amendments rest on ISS alone and differ in detail from Al Jazeera's account of a parliamentary vote on the Elections Act.
The dissolution date of 22 September is inferred from the Al Jazeera article's reference to a Tuesday decree in a piece dated 23 September.
Displacement figures differ (UN Commission 3.2 million, UNHCR 1.3 million internally displaced); the counting methods were not reconciled.
Oil, pound and poverty figures come from Eye Radio's secondary analysis ('reportedly'); the IMF and World Bank primary documents for 2026 were not opened.
Both The East African article and the UN Commission's Geneva report were read through excerpts; the full reports were not opened.
No podcast episode on South Sudan was verified; the VOA South Sudan in Focus page showed no playable episodes. Only one documentary was verified.
The Machar trial has no reporting in this draft later than 5 September 2026 in search results; the current state of proceedings is unknown.
